TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
TUESDAY, 28 FEBRUARY 2023 AT 10:02 AM (AEST)
DAY 38
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MR ANGUS SCOTT KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MR DOUGLAS FREEBURN, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MS GEORGINA COSTELLO KC, for Renee Leon
MS CARYN VAN PROCTOR, for Renee Leon
MR GUY REYNOLDS SC, for the Hon Michael Keenan
MR DANIEL WARD, for the Hon Michael Keenan

COMMISSIONER: Right. Today's appearances?
MR GREGGERY: Today I appear with Mr Freeburn of Counsel.
COMMISSIONER: Thanks, Mr Greggery. Ms Hogan-Doran?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: May it please the Commission. Today I appear for the Commonwealth. I
do not have any juniors with me - - -
COMMISSIONER: All by yourself?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: All by myself.
COMMISSIONER: Thanks. And Ms Costello, I think.
MS COSTELLO: May it please the Commission. I appear with Ms van Proctor for Professor
Leon.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Yes. Sorry, and?
MR REYNOLDS: May it please the Commission. I appear for Mr Keenan with my learned
friend Mr Ward.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you, Mr Reynolds. Now, did you want to stay while Ms Leon - I
suppose there might be something of interest to you in Ms Leon's examination.
MR REYNOLDS: Possibly, but could we be given a marking if that's - - -
COMMISSIONER: Could you what, sorry?
MR REYNOLDS: Be given a marking, a not before - - -
COMMISSIONER: If you would prefer that. Can you indicate when you think this witness
might be done, roughly?
MR GREGGERY: By lunchtime, but it's possible by 12 or 12.30 also. So a not before midday
would be - - -
COMMISSIONER: Yes. My experience with Counsel is add two hours to that. So we will make
it not before midday, if that suits you, Mr Reynolds.
MR REYNOLDS: Thank you.

MR GREGGERY: Thank you, Commissioner. The witness this morning is Professor Leon, who is
present.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Did you have exhibits?
MR GREGGERY: I do. I will tender those relating to Ms Leon only and leave the balance for
Mr Scott. The draft exhibit list contains numbers 6040 and the extent of exhibits relevant to
Professor Leon's evidence concludes at 6124.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. The items bearing the numbers 6040 to 6124 are admitted according
to the numbers they bear in that schedule.
<EXHIBITS 6040 TO 6124 TENDERED AS PER THE EXHIBIT LIST
COMMISSIONER: Now, Professor Leon, would you prefer to take an oath or an affirmation?
PROFESSOR LEON: An affirmation, thank you, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. Thanks. If you would stand, that will be administered now.
<RENEE ELMINA LEON, AFFIRMED
<EXAMINATION BY MR GREGGERY
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you, Commissioner. Might I address you as Ms Leon?
PROFESSOR LEON: Certainly.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. Can you tell the Commission your full name, please?
PROFESSOR LEON: Renee Elmina Leon.
MR GREGGERY: And, Ms Leon, you are currently the Vice Chancellor of Charles Sturt
University?
PROFESSOR LEON: I am.
MR GREGGERY: You were served with a Notice to Give a Statement and Produce Documents,
NTG-0044, dated 23 December 2022, and you have produced two Statements in response,
the first dated 23 November 2022 and the second dated 20 February 2023. Is that correct?
PROFESSOR LEON: Yes.

PROFESSOR LEON: They are.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. Ms Leon, you commenced as the Secretary for the Department of
Human Services in October 2018. Is that correct?
PROFESSOR LEON: 2017.
MR GREGGERY: '17, sorry.
PROFESSOR LEON: I commenced in the role several weeks before that. I was appointed to
the role in September 2017, but I was on leave until the 9th of October 2017. So I effectively
commenced in the role at that time.
MR GREGGERY: Prior to commencing in that role, you had been for some time the Secretary
of a different Department; that's right?
PROFESSOR LEON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: That’s right? I know that you are nodding. It's just being recorded, So - - -
PROFESSOR LEON: I'm sorry.
MR GREGGERY: That's okay. And that was the Department of Employment?
PROFESSOR LEON: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: And in your role as Secretary for the Department of Employment, you came
to know your predecessor, Kathryn Campbell?
PROFESSOR LEON: I had known Kathryn Campbell for many years. We were both senior
public servants. She had been a Deputy Secretary in the Department of Finance, so I knew
her when I was a Deputy Secretary also. And then she was the Secretary of the Department
of Human Services throughout the time that I was the Secretary of the Department of
Employment.
MR GREGGERY: And you outline in your Statement a very long career as a public servant in
the Commonwealth Public Service?
PROFESSOR LEON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Which commenced, I think you say, in the Attorney-General's Department. Is
that right?
PROFESSOR LEON: That's right.

PROFESSOR LEON: 1990 or '91, I think.
MR GREGGERY: In terms of your professional qualifications, you hold a Bachelor of Arts and a
Bachelor of Laws from the Australian National University?
PROFESSOR LEON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And a Master of Laws from the University of Cambridge?
PROFESSOR LEON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Specialised in international law?
PROFESSOR LEON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And in your - in the senior roles you set out in your Statement, that is, senior
roles within the Australian Public Service, you set out a role as a Deputy Secretary of the
Attorney-General's Department from 2009 to 2011; a Deputy Secretary of the Department of
Prime Minister and Cabinet from 2011 to 2013; and then the Secretary role within with the
Department of Employment from 2013 to 2017?
PROFESSOR LEON: Yes, that's correct.
MR GREGGERY: And your - the period of time for which you were Secretary of the
Department of Human Services ended in December 2019?
PROFESSOR LEON: My appointment was terminated at the end of January 2020, but I was on
leave for the last month. So my last effective date was the 24th of December 2019.
MR GREGGERY: In terms of your relationship with Ms Campbell prior to you taking over the
role at the Department of Human Services, how would you characterise it?
PROFESSOR LEON: Collegial.
MR GREGGERY: Did it remain collegial while you were the Secretary of that Department as
she was the Secretary of the Department of Social Services?
PROFESSOR LEON: It became more difficult.
MR GREGGERY: Was that a progressive change to the relationship?
PROFESSOR LEON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Can you recall any particular point at which you first noticed some difficulty?
Is there anything that stands out in your mind?

PROFESSOR LEON: There wasn't a particular point where it suddenly changed, but certainly
by early to mid 2019 it was very difficult.
MR GREGGERY: Did those difficulties centre on any particular topic or were they across a
range of your interactions on different topics?
PROFESSOR LEON: I would characterise the difficulties that began to emerge in the
relationship as being ones that arose because of two factors. One was that the Department
of Human Services was the service delivery agency for a considerable number of other
Commonwealth agencies, including the Department of Social Services, of which Ms Campbell
was Secretary. And nevertheless - notwithstanding the fact that the Department of Human
Services is responsible for service delivery, the Secretary of the Department of Social Services
felt that it may come to reverberate upon her if anything in the delivery of social services
was not up to par.
And so she was concerned, if ever there was criticism about Social Services programs that
could be attributed to the Department of Human Services, then there was sometimes, I think
regrettably and unnecessarily, a desire to attribute blame. I should say I had relationships
with a broad range of other department heads with whom I had the same responsibilities to
deliver their services, most significantly the Department of Health, for which I delivered all of
the Medicare services. But those relationships were entirely collegial, and we approached
our shared responsibilities in a shared fashion.
MR GREGGERY: That is, even in circumstances where there may be some criticism of the
delivery of services for the Department of Health, there was a proactive and positive
approach to resolving - - -
PROFESSOR LEON: That's correct.
MR GREGGERY: - - - whatever the issue was in respect of the service question?
PROFESSOR LEON: That's correct. For example, there was a very well publicised data breach
out of Medicare at one stage, but there was never any attitude of blame as between me and
the Department of Health. We worked together to resolve it.
MR GREGGERY: Did those increasing difficulties in the relationship with Ms Campbell during
2019 have a limiting effect on the level of free communication that might - you might have
hoped for?
PROFESSOR LEON: I was always aware that I had to be careful about how I raised issues with
Ms Campbell. I should say, I'm a long-standing public servant and I was committed to
discharging my duties professionally and appropriately. So we conducted ourselves
professionally at all times, both me and Ms Campbell. There certainly weren't - there weren't
displays of unprofessional behaviour. I was aware, not only from my own observations but
also from matters that other people raised with me, that at times when I wasn't present, it
was possible things were being said about me that were designed to undermine my

MR GREGGERY: That is, things said by Ms Campbell - - -
PROFESSOR LEON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: - - - in the presence of others, but not you?
PROFESSOR LEON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And was that reported to you by the Minister - - -
PROFESSOR LEON: No.
MR GREGGERY: - - - or the Minister's advisers or people within your Department?
PROFESSOR LEON: People within my Department and people external to the Department.
MR GREGGERY: Those who were external to the Department, where did they fit in the
Commonwealth Public Service?
PROFESSOR LEON: So one of those was a former Secretary who was still undertaking
occasional consulting work for the Commonwealth, and another was a former Secretary who
was involved in mentoring people in the Public Service in senior roles and who had therefore
many connections throughout the Public Service.
MR GREGGERY: And the reports to you of those statements by Ms Campbell, did they reflect
a criticism about your performance or your ability?
PROFESSOR LEON: They, I think, could be characterised as reflecting both criticism about the
way in which I was undertaking the duties of Secretary of the Department of Human Services
and the extent of my responsiveness to the policy goals of the then government.
MR GREGGERY: And when you say, "the extent of your responsiveness", something is
conveyed then being less than fully responsive to policy goals, I take it?
PROFESSOR LEON: That's right. How it was put to me, I suppose, in general terms rather than
having specific words that had been said conveyed to me, was that it was put to me that
there was a - an attempt to undermine me in my relationship with the Minister and the
government.
MR GREGGERY: Right.
PROFESSOR LEON: But I do want to emphasis that this was only an undercurrent in the
background in terms of my conducting the duties of my role. I conducted the duties of my
role professionally, thoroughly. I engaged with Ms Campbell at all times professionally and
collegiately, and - and we conducted ourselves entirely professionally and appropriately in

MR GREGGERY: That is, throughout your long career in the Public Service, the potential for
interpersonal interactions to become uncomfortable or, it seems, challenging from time to
time was not unknown to you, but it was important from your perspective to maintain that
high degree of professionalism you've just described?
PROFESSOR LEON: It was not unknown to me, but it was certainly unusual for me. I think
people throughout the Public Service would pretty uniformly describe me as a highly
collegiate leader, and I had good relationships with many Secretaries and Deputy Secretaries
across the Commonwealth. And I think were you to ask almost any other witness who
appears here, they would describe me as being well known for being collegiate. So I hadn't
had a history of difficult interpersonal relationships. And in general, at the senior levels of
the Public Service, we are all expected to not let personal matters affect anything to do with
the performance of our duties.
And I don't think there was anything interpersonal about my relationship with Kathryn. She
and I had been good colleagues. We had been the kind of colleagues who called each other
to chat after Secretaries Board. We had been on overseas work trips together where we had
been on good terms, not just cool professional terms. I would have said we were colleagues.
So I was surprised to find an element of tension in the relationship by 2019. And I wondered
at that time if it was not seeking to undermine me, but a - perhaps a kind of - some
unhappiness about the fact that I was now running a Department that she had run for a long
time and had certain views about and perhaps found it difficult to see someone else running
it differently.
COMMISSIONER: You said there were two factors that made the relationship difficult. Was
that the second one or - - -
PROFESSOR LEON: No. Thank you, Commissioner, for reminding me of that. The second
factor that made the relationship difficult arose after Mr Robert became the Minister for
Government Services and responsible for my portfolio, and Minister Robert had very
significant plans for the portfolio. And I didn't realise at the beginning, but it became
apparent to me during the course of his development of those plans that Ms Campbell was
speaking to him directly about that and was keen on progressing the Minister's plan, which
would have involved very far-reaching and, in my view, difficult to implement changes to the
portfolio. And Ms Campbell was encouraging and actively supporting the development of
those plans, which would have involved the dismemberment of the Department. So then
there became a question on which we were taking a different view but that I understood she
was directly engaging with my Minister about.
COMMISSIONER: What were the plans? Can you give us a summary?
PROFESSOR LEON: Minister Robert wanted to break the Department of Human Services into
four separate agencies to deal with the constituent parts of IT and service delivery and
compliance and design, and to put those all underneath a single sort of small parent
Department. And his plan appeared to be motivated by what he had seen in New South

Wales where Service NSW was created as an agency that only did the service delivery, not
any of the compliance or design.
And, of course, the Department of Human Services is quite a different beast to Service NSW
and couldn't have progressed the plan that the Minister was proposing without very
considerable impact on service delivery. So I was in the position that sometimes is
unfortunate for a public servant to be in of having to give the Minister advice that something
he was keen to do had some difficulties with it. And so then there was the problem of finding
that I was the - you know, the bad cop, as it were, advising against the policy, whereas Ms
Campbell was encouraging and promoting the idea of the Minister.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MR GREGGERY: How would the implementation of that concept, that broad proposal, affect
the functions of DSS, if at all?
PROFESSOR LEON: Well, it didn't develop far enough to know what would have happened
about that. But I believe that it's what led to the plan that was eventually implemented,
which was to make the Department of Human Services a subsidiary agency under the
Department of Social Services. So when it became apparent that dismantling the Department
into four parts wasn't actually possible and couldn't achieve the industrial relations
outcomes that the Minister wanted, which - you may know that when Service NSW was
established, all of the precursor agencies - the staff had to reapply for their jobs so that
people who weren't appropriately oriented towards service delivery could be replaced with
people who were felt to have the right attitude and culture, and you could get a new
enterprise agreement without all of those problematic public service conditions and so on.
And so the Minister had to be advised not only by me but by others in the Public Service it
wasn't - it wasn't possible to just dismiss everyone in Human Services and still keep service
delivery running, for example. So some of the aims that were sought to be achieved couldn't
be achieved, but what then was developed, though not in any consultation with me - in fact,
the first I knew of it was when I was told my position was to be abolished because my
Department was to be abolished - was for Human Services to become Services Australia as a
subsidiary of the Department of Social Services.
MR GREGGERY: And when were you informed of that?
PROFESSOR LEON: The 4th of December 2019. It was announced on the 5th of December.
MR GREGGERY: Right.
COMMISSIONER: And were you one of the people whose attitude wasn't appropriate?
PROFESSOR LEON: We were never given a reason for our termination, Commissioner, but I
did think that there was some commonality amongst the five Secretaries who were
terminated, which was that we did believe in frank and fearless advice.

MR GREGGERY: Just on that topic, Ms Leon, the provision of frank and fearless advice, one of
the observations or comments you make in your Statements is that there was a tendency or
an unstated practice to provide difficult advice to Ministers orally.
PROFESSOR LEON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Can you elaborate on that? Was that always the case from the point at
which you commenced in - as Secretary of DHS?
PROFESSOR LEON: I would have said that that was the case when I was the Secretary of
Employment, as well as when I was the Secretary of DHS. But it certainly became more and
more pronounced in more recent years, and there was much more visible feelings that there
were consequences for people if they were unhelpful to the government. So people became
more anxious to be seen as compliant with Ministers' expectations about how things would
be done. But there had been, I think, a long-standing and undesirable practice for things that
were problematic not to be written down. And, in fact, Peter Shergold conducted the inquiry
into the Home Insulation Scheme, and one of his findings was that it turned out lots of things
hadn't been written down about pink batts, they had just been done orally and he said that
should stop. But it hasn't.
MR GREGGERY: And it continued to be a practice, as I understand your evidence, up to the
point at which you ceased in the role?
PROFESSOR LEON: Well, I refer in my evidence to having to increasingly put things in writing
at the end. But you did know as a senior public servant that once you had got to the point
where you had to put difficult things in writing, that that was because you were potentially
on a collision course with your Minister and, therefore, it was essential to document what
was happening. And the fact that we all - that I approached that with the degree of
realisation of its seriousness that I was now putting these things in writing, I suppose reflects
the fact that it had become relatively uncommon to put disagreements or difficulties in
writing.
Sometimes we put them in writing but in a euphemistic way. So instead of saying, "This
policy will cause significant hardship," you might be expected to say something more like,
"This policy will cause community concern.” So that were the matter to come out under
freedom of information at a later stage, the Minister couldn't be accused of having turned a
blind eye to the fact of significant hardship.
I should say there was another reason why matters sometimes were done verbally - and this
is also referred to in my Statement - which is that when things are written down in the
Commonwealth, even in matters that you would think are relatively tightly held, like matters
that are going to Cabinet, they actually have quite a broad distribution. So a lot of people will
see them. So if there are matters that you want to keep quite close just to those with a need
to know, sometimes it's only possible to do that by conveying the information verbally.

MR GREGGERY: You refer at one point to a potential information leak in 2019. That's an
example of the broad distribution of sensitive material and the difficulty knowing quite
where a leak might come from?
PROFESSOR LEON: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: If we return to the chronology. When you commenced as Secretary, you
were provided with an Incoming Secretary Brief dated October 2017?
PROFESSOR LEON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: In the two volumes of documents that are to your right, this document
appears behind tab 4 in the first volume. It is Exhibit 6225, which I don't think I have
tendered. But you will see on - it covers a broad range of high-level issues that you needed to
be appraised of in the mind of the Department as you commenced the role.
PROFESSOR LEON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Sorry, 6213. The question in respect of the information provided in relation
to the compliance program is addressed at paragraph 2.33 and following on page 9. The
document is CTH.3003.0001.0009. Do you have page 9 of the document?
PROFESSOR LEON: I do.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you, Ms Leon. What was said to you by the Department through this
Brief was, in effect, that the Online Compliance debt recovery measure that was introduced
in a manual way in July 2015 and then in an automated or online fashion in July 2016 was
essentially a long-standing practice despite the criticisms of it that had taken place.
PROFESSOR LEON: I think I was told two things by this Brief: one, that it was a long-standing
practice consistent with the Department's assessment of debts over many years; but,
secondly, that there had been concern and criticism of the rollout that was primarily about
how it had been done, that we should have prepared better, that we should have taken
more account of the customer experience, that kind of thing.
MR GREGGERY: One of the critical assertions in the document in terms of information you
were given appears at the top of page 10 where it says:
The portal did not change how data matching was undertaken or the way income was
assessed, and differences calculated.
Do you see that?
PROFESSOR LEON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Did you understand, then, from a very early stage in your role at DHS that

PROFESSOR LEON: I didn't even know there was a question about the lawfulness of the
Scheme that I needed to have confidence or not confidence about at that stage. I understood
that it was an unpopular scheme, but I didn't have anything brought to my attention that led
me to think there were doubts about whether it was lawful.
MR GREGGERY: And you were only aware, I take it, prior to October 2017, of criticisms of the
Scheme in general terms that you may have picked up through the media?
PROFESSOR LEON: That's right. It may have been mentioned, and I expect it would have been
mentioned, at regular meetings of the Secretaries Board where from time to time Secretaries
would mention anything significant that was happening in their portfolio. So it's possible that
I knew Kathryn Campbell was managing the response to this Scheme at the time that it
became controversial, but I didn't - I didn't know anything about the nature of it.
MR GREGGERY: Another feature of the information provided was that there was an
investigation by the Commonwealth Ombudsman earlier that year, but the conclusion of that
investigation was stated that:
The Ombudsman did, however, find the system could accurately calculate debts, providing
reassurance that debt calculations were consistent with the previous manual process.
PROFESSOR LEON: That's right. And that was asserted to me not only in this Brief but
regularly in other material. So, for example, every time I attended Senate estimates, words
to that effect would be provided in my talking points.
MR GREGGERY: And in that sense, the Department relied on the conclusions reached by the
Ombudsman in that investigation in respect of any ongoing criticisms about the accuracy of
calculation of debts at the least?
PROFESSOR LEON: They relied on it for the purposes of further bolstering the position that
the system was appropriate and proper in its foundation, but I think they did genuinely
believe that it was.
MR GREGGERY: The - from the evidence that you have given about not even being aware
that there was a legal question about the Scheme, I will have two documents shown to you. I
don't expect you have ever seen these, but I would like to clarify that point. They are Exhibits
5106A, CTH.3007.0004.3601, and Exhibit 5107, CTH.3007.0004.3602. These two emails were
sent and received in January 2017, well in advance of your commencement as Secretary later
that year. The first in the sequence is the Exhibit 5107, which appears on the right of the
screen. It is an email from Glyn Fiveash to Tracy Tozer dated 11 January 2017 about social
security debts and the calculation of them. Can I confirm firstly that you have no recollection
of ever seeing this document?
PROFESSOR LEON: I have never seen it.

MR GREGGERY: And you may peruse it yourself briefly, but it was the subject of my opening
address at this Hearing Block last Monday. And the advice was to the effect that the
Department could not apply an income amount received over a larger period, for example,
12 months, in any way against a customer other than in the manner in which the person
received it in those individual fortnights, that is, the annual amount cannot simply be divided
by 26 and applied as the person's income over 26 payment fortnights. There is the loose use
of the word "apportioned" in the last sentence, but the intent - or the advice remains
unchanged, that is, that:
The amount needs to be apportioned between the relevant fortnights in the period at the
rate at which it was actually earned, derived or received.
My emphasise on the word "actually". The other document you have is on the left, and it is
an email from Ms Musolino to various persons who hold General Counsel or similar positions
within DHS, dated 23 January 2017, in which she requests any legal advices, either internal or
external, provided by Legal to the business regarding debt recovery of Centrelink
overpayments and specially about the Online Compliance system. And in response on 23
January 2017, Mr Fiveash sent the previous document that he had provided to a different
area about two weeks earlier. I take it you haven't seen that document either?
PROFESSOR LEON: I haven't. And it's a surprise to me that these documents exist because, as
I indicated in my Statement, towards the end, once it was apparent that the program was
unlawful, I asked the Legal Services Division to do an excavation because I couldn't
understand how the Department had been so misadvised to have implemented the program
all along. So I did ask them to do an examination of what advice, if any, had been sought or
generated. And this advice did not get unearthed in that excavation, which I've referred to in
my Statement.
MR GREGGERY: That excavation was carried out by Ms Keeling, I think?
PROFESSOR LEON: That's right. Under some time pressure, I'm sure.
MR GREGGERY: Undoubtedly. To your knowledge, did she speak with Ms Musolino?
PROFESSOR LEON: I think that she said she had undertaken the excavation both by file
search and by speaking to relevant officers who were still in the Department. I'm fairly
certain she said that she hadn't contacted people who were no longer in the Department,
but she didn't refer by name to the particular people that she spoke to.
MR GREGGERY: Do I understand the effect of your evidence to remain that at no stage did
Ms Musolino ever communicate to you that she was aware of advice from within the
Department which raised at least a question about the legality of averaging?
PROFESSOR LEON: That's correct.
MR GREGGERY: And that wasn't for want of the topic not coming up?

PROFESSOR LEON: It didn't come up at the beginning because I didn't know it was a live
issue, or should be an issue. But when it was brought to my attention that there were
questions about legality, I did expressly ask Ms Musolino whether we were confident the
program was lawful.
MR GREGGERY: Before I move on from that very early period, returning to the Incoming
Secretary Brief, there was - rather, information was provided in that Brief which related to
the workforce of the Department. And one of those points was the potential engagement of
1,000 non-APS contractors to complete compliance measure activities and the potential
Budget underspend if those persons were not employed. What do you recall of the
engagement of non-APS employees in the Department during your period as Secretary and
the role that they played?
PROFESSOR LEON: There were - there were two main ways in which - or roles in which
non-APS people were employed for the work of the Department. One was for general service
delivery, primarily answering the telephone, because the workforce of Human Services had
been being steadily reduced by the government under the effects of the efficiency dividend,
such that inevitably the Department had to lose about 1,000 staff every year. And since the
largest part of the Department was service delivery, no amount of increased efficiency had
been able to entirely absorb the impact of that. So people were waiting a very long time for
things like getting through on the telephone. So we were on a pathway to engage labour hire
to supplement the workforce for answering the phone because that would be consistent
with the government's policy to reduce APS numbers, even though it wasn't reducing the
actual number of people.
The second area was not derived from the reductions caused by the efficiency dividend, and
that was the compliance area. And the reason for the need for additional personnel in this
space was because they had - the government had, prior to my arriving, realised that the
way in which the Online Compliance program had been designed assumed that it would
nearly all be done online with very little need for people to speak to a person in the
Department. And the difficulties with implementation that occurred in late 2016 and early
2017 led to the government having to revise that idea and enable people to ring up and
speak to someone. But they didn't want - the government didn't want to increase Public
Service numbers for this role, so the work was to be undertaken by labour hire. So that may
have been referred to as the C1000 in some of the documents that existed.
MR GREGGERY: And was the C - - -
PROFESSOR LEON: For compliance.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. Yes. For the document operator, we were at the bottom of page
8, .0020, and the top of page 9, .0021. At the top of page 9, there is a reference to the
Minister's expectation that:
…following certification of the proposed Agreement in October 2017, these changes will be
accelerated...

That is a reference to the changes in the dot points on the previous page. And:
if not, the department faces a potential underspend in the financial year of some $200 million
with a corresponding impact on service delivery.
PROFESSOR LEON: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: That question of contractors rather than employment of APS persons
appears to me to be picked up again at page 34, .0048, under 4.2, Financial Information and
ASL.
PROFESSOR LEON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And ASL is average staffing level, I take it?
PROFESSOR LEON: That's correct.
MR GREGGERY: And was that the quota or cap imposed by the government in respect of the
employment of permanent Public Service staff within the Department?
PROFESSOR LEON: That's correct. The ASL cap reflected how many public servants could be
employed, but it didn't - and increasingly didn't - align with the Budget, because the Budget
was allocated to deliver a certain level of service. Just couldn't employ public servants to do
it.
